claim: A temporal latency code represents odor identity in olfactory bulb (OB).
source: A temporal latency code represents odor identity in olfactory bulb (OB), but this temporal information is discarded in piriform cortex (PCx) where odor identity is instead encoded through ensemble membership.
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies on OB coding

claim: Temporal information is discarded in piriform cortex (PCx) where odor identity is instead encoded through ensemble membership.
source: A temporal latency code represents odor identity in olfactory bulb (OB), but this temporal information is discarded in piriform cortex (PCx) where odor identity is instead encoded through ensemble membership.
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies on PCx coding

claim: The impact of OB inputs activated earliest after inhalation is amplified within PCx by diffuse recurrent collateral excitation.
source: In the model, the impact of OB inputs activated earliest after inhalation is amplified within PCx by diffuse recurrent collateral excitation, which then recruits strong, sustained feedback inhibition that suppresses the impact of later-responding glomeruli.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model presented in the manuscript

claim: Recurrent collateral excitation recruits strong, sustained feedback inhibition that suppresses the impact of later-responding glomeruli.
source: In the model, the impact of OB inputs activated earliest after inhalation is amplified within PCx by diffuse recurrent collateral excitation, which then recruits strong, sustained feedback inhibition that suppresses the impact of later-responding glomeruli.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model presented in the manuscript

claim: Increasing odor concentrations is modeled by decreasing glomerulus onset latencies while preserving their activation sequences.
source: We model increasing odor concentrations by decreasing glomerulus onset latencies while preserving their activation sequences.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used in the study

claim: The model produces a multiplexed cortical odor code in which activated ensembles are robust to concentration changes while concentration information is encoded through population synchrony.
source: This produces a multiplexed cortical odor code in which activated ensembles are robust to concentration changes while concentration information is encoded through population synchrony.
evidence: This is a key finding from the computational model

claim: A latency code is thought to be used in olfactory bulb (OB) to represent odor identity.
source: In olfaction, a latency code is thought to be used in olfactory bulb (OB) to represent odor identity (Bathellier et al., 2008; Cury and Uchida, 2010; Shusterman et al., 2011; Gschwend et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental studies

claim: Olfactory information is transformed into a spatially distributed ensemble in primary olfactory (piriform) cortex (PCx).
source: This information is transformed into a spatially distributed ensemble in primary olfactory (piriform) cortex (PCx) (Uchida et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study

claim: PCx is a three-layered cortex with well-characterized circuitry.
source: PCx is a three-layered cortex with well-characterized circuitry (Bekkers and Suzuki, 2013), providing an advantageous system to mechanistically dissect this transformation.
evidence: Supported by citation to anatomical study

claim: Each OSN expresses just one of ~1000 different odorant receptor genes.
source: Each OSN expresses just one of ~1000 different odorant receptor genes (Buck and Axel, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to foundational study

claim: Odorant receptors are broadly tuned so that OSN firing rates reflect their receptor's affinity for a given odorant and the odorant concentration.
source: Odorant receptors are broadly tuned so that OSN firing rates reflect their receptor's affinity for a given odorant and the odorant concentration (Malnic et al., 1999; Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: All OSNs expressing a given receptor converge on a unique pair of OB glomeruli.
source: All OSNs expressing a given receptor converge on a unique pair of OB glomeruli (Mombaerts et al., 1996), where they make excitatory synaptic connections onto dendrites of mitral/tufted cells (MTCs), the sole output neurons of the OB.
evidence: Supported by citation to anatomical study

claim: MTCs are the sole output neurons of the OB.
source: All OSNs expressing a given receptor converge on a unique pair of OB glomeruli (Mombaerts et al., 1996), where they make excitatory synaptic connections onto dendrites of mitral/tufted cells (MTCs), the sole output neurons of the OB.
evidence: This is established knowledge about OB anatomy

claim: Each MTC only receives excitatory input from one glomerulus.
source: Because each MTC only receives excitatory input from one glomerulus, each MTC essentially encodes the activation of a single class of odorant receptor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about OB anatomy

claim: MTCs exhibit subthreshold, respiration-coupled membrane potential oscillations.
source: MTCs exhibit subthreshold, respiration-coupled membrane potential oscillations (Cang and Isaacson, 2003; Margrie and Schaefer, 2003) that may help transform rate-coded OSN input into a temporal latency code in the OB (Hopfield, 1995; Schaefer et al., 2006; Schaefer and Margrie, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: Respiration-coupled membrane potential oscillations may help transform rate-coded OSN input into a temporal latency code in the OB.
source: MTCs exhibit subthreshold, respiration-coupled membrane potential oscillations (Cang and Isaacson, 2003; Margrie and Schaefer, 2003) that may help transform rate-coded OSN input into a temporal latency code in the OB (Hopfield, 1995; Schaefer et al., 2006; Schaefer and Margrie, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical and experimental studies

claim: Individual MTC responses exhibit odor-specific latencies that tile the ~300–500 ms respiration (sniff) cycle.
source: Individual MTC responses exhibit odor-specific latencies that tile the ~300–500 ms respiration (sniff) cycle (Bathellier et al., 2008; Cury and Uchida, 2010; Shusterman et al., 2011; Gschwend et al., 2012), and decoding analyses indicate that spike time information is required to accurately represent odor identity in the OB (Cury and Uchida, 2010; Junek et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: Spike time information is required to accurately represent odor identity in the OB.
source: Individual MTC responses exhibit odor-specific latencies that tile the ~300–500 ms respiration (sniff) cycle (Bathellier et al., 2008; Cury and Uchida, 2010; Shusterman et al., 2011; Gschwend et al., 2012), and decoding analyses indicate that spike time information is required to accurately represent odor identity in the OB (Cury and Uchida, 2010; Junek et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: The OB uses a temporal code to represent odor identity.
source: Thus, the OB uses a temporal code to represent odor identity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from cited experimental evidence

claim: MTC projections to PCx are diffuse and overlapping.
source: Olfactory information is conveyed to PCx via MTC projections that are diffuse and overlapping (Ghosh et al., 2011; Miyamichi et al., 2011; Sosulski et al., 2011), ensuring that individual PCx principal neurons receive inputs from different combinations of co-activated glomeruli (Franks and Isaacson, 2006; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2006; Apicella et al., 2010; Davison and Ehlers, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies

claim: Individual PCx principal neurons receive inputs from different combinations of co-activated glomeruli.
source: Olfactory information is conveyed to PCx via MTC projections that are diffuse and overlapping (Ghosh et al., 2011; Miyamichi et al., 2011; Sosulski et al., 2011), ensuring that individual PCx principal neurons receive inputs from different combinations of co-activated glomeruli (Franks and Isaacson, 2006; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2006; Apicella et al., 2010; Davison and Ehlers, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: Odors activate distinct ensembles of neurons distributed across PCx.
source: Consequently, odors activate distinct ensembles of neurons distributed across PCx (Illig and Haberly, 2003; Rennaker et al., 2007; Stettler and Axel, 2009; Roland et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: Odor identity in PCx is encoded simply by the specific ensembles of cells activated during the sniff, with no additional information provided by spike timing.
source: Recent studies indicate that odor identity in PCx is encoded simply by the specific ensembles of cells activated during the sniff, with no additional information provided by spike timing (Miura et al., 2012; Bolding and Franks, 2017).

claim: A temporal odor code in OB is transformed into an ensemble code in PCx.
source: Thus, a temporal odor code in OB is transformed into an ensemble code in PCx.

claim: PCx ensembles are sensitive to the sequence in which glomeruli are activated.
source: However, these ensembles are sensitive to the sequence in which glomeruli are activated (Haddad et al., 2013), indicating that PCx could parse temporally structured OB input.

claim: MTCs respond throughout the respiration cycle.

claim: Most odor-activated PCx cells respond transiently, shortly after inhalation.

claim: Cortical odor responses are preferentially defined by the earliest-active glomeruli.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that cortical odor responses are preferentially defined by the earliest-active glomeruli and that glomeruli activated later in the sniff are relatively ineffective at driving responses.

claim: Glomeruli activated later in the sniff are relatively ineffective at driving PCx responses.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that cortical odor responses are preferentially defined by the earliest-active glomeruli and that glomeruli activated later in the sniff are relatively ineffective at driving responses.

claim: Activity was much sparser in PCx than in OB, with most responsive cells spiking within 50 ms of inhalation.

claim: Odors evoked a sustained increase in MTC spiking throughout the sniff.

claim: Spiking activity in PCx peaks briefly after inhalation followed by a period of sustained suppression.

claim: A spatio-temporal code for odor identity in OB is transformed into an ensemble code in PCx in which the cortical ensemble is largely defined by the earliest-active OB inputs.

claim: Information conveyed by later-responding OB inputs is discounted in PCx.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data and cited literature

claim: Total OB output is sustained and can even grow over time.
source: Because total OB output is sustained and can even grow over time, suppression of later responses must originate from inhibition within PCx itself.

source: Because total OB output is sustained and can even grow over time, suppression of later responses must originate from inhibition within PCx itself.

source: Pyramidal cells also form a widespread recurrent collateral excitatory plexus that, in turn, recruits strong feedback inhibition (FBI) from a distinct class of layer 2/3 interneurons (Stokes and Isaacson, 2010; Franks et al., 2011; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2012; Large et al., 2016), and this intracortical recurrent circuitry is thought to contribute substantially to odor-evoked cortical responses (Davison and Ehlers, 2011; Poo and Isaacson, 2011; Haddad et al., 2013).

claim: Intracortical recurrent circuitry is thought to contribute substantially to odor-evoked cortical responses.
source: Pyramidal cells also form a widespread recurrent collateral excitatory plexus that, in turn, recruits strong feedback inhibition (FBI) from a distinct class of layer 2/3 interneurons (Stokes and Isaacson, 2010; Franks et al., 2011; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2012; Large et al., 2016), and this intracortical recurrent circuitry is thought to contribute substantially to odor-evoked cortical responses (Davison and Ehlers, 2011; Poo and Isaacson, 2011; Haddad et al., 2013).

claim: Low levels of spontaneous PCx spiking in the model are driven by baseline activity in mitral cells.
source: Low levels of spontaneous PCx spiking in the model are driven by baseline activity in mitral cells, and 2.8 ± 0.4% (mean ± st. dev) of pyramidal cells spike during the 200 ms inhalation in the absence of odor, consistent with spontaneous firing observed in anesthetized rats (Poo and Isaacson, 2009) and near, but slightly lower than, spontaneous rates in awake animals (Zhan and Luo, 2010; Miura et al., 2012; Bolding and Franks, 2017; Iurilli and Datta, 2017).

claim: 2.8 ± 0.4% (mean ± st. dev) of pyramidal cells spike during the 200 ms inhalation in the absence of odor in the model.
